ap_physics_1-m01.stem: A person pulls a suitcase along a level floor with a strap that makes an angle of $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. The tension in the strap is $60\text{ N}$ and the suitcase moves $4\text{ m}$ along the floor. How much work does the strap's tension do on the suitcase?

options.why: Divides by the cosine instead of multiplying, $Fd/\cos\theta$.
Uses the sine of the angle (the vertical component of the force), $Fd\sin\theta$.
Only the horizontal component does work: $W=Fd\cos\theta=60\times4\times\cos40^\circ=184\text{ J}$.
Ignores the angle and multiplies the full tension by the distance, $Fd$.

blueprint.concept: Work done by a force that is not parallel to the displacement
student_thinking: Find the component of the force along the displacement

key_conditions.condition: only the component of the force along the displacement does work
key_conditions.evidence: the strap pulls at an angle above the horizontal along a level floor

misconceptions.description: Divides by the cosine instead of multiplying, $Fd/\cos\theta$.
Uses the sine of the angle (the vertical component of the force), $Fd\sin\theta$.
Ignores the angle and multiplies the full tension by the distance, $Fd$.

verification.independent_path: the work is recomputed as the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector in numpy

options.why: Ignores the angle and multiplies the full tension by the distance, $Fd$.

ap_physics_1-m02.stem: A $10\text{ kg}$ crate starts at rest on a level floor. A worker pushes it with a constant horizontal force of $100\text{ N}$ for $6\text{ m}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is $0.4$. What is the speed of the crate after it has moved $6\text{ m}$?

options.why: Uses the work done by friction alone as the net work, $\sqrt{2fd/m}$.
Divides the net work by the mass but never takes the square root.
Friction is $\mu mg=39.2$ N, so $W_{net}=(100-39.2)\times6=365$ J and $\tfrac12mv^2=W_{net}$ gives $v=8.54$ m/s.
Sets the net work equal to $mv^2$ instead of $\tfrac12mv^2$, giving $\sqrt{W_{net}/m}$.

blueprint.concept: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy
student_thinking: Compute the net force as the applied force minus kinetic friction
Set the net work equal to the kinetic energy gained and solve for the speed

key_conditions.condition: the crate starts from rest and friction is constant
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives rest and a constant coefficient of kinetic friction

misconceptions.description: Uses the work done by friction alone as the net work, $\sqrt{2fd/m}$.
Divides the net work by the mass but never takes the square root.
Sets the net work equal to $mv^2$ instead of $\tfrac12mv^2$, giving $\sqrt{W_{net}/m}$.

ap_physics_1-m03.stem: A $1.5\text{ kg}$ block is released from rest at a height of $0.4\text{ m}$ directly above a light vertical spring of spring constant $200\text{ N/m}$ standing on the floor. The block lands on the spring and compresses it. What is the maximum compression of the spring? Ignore air resistance.

options.why: Drops the factor of one half in the spring energy, $x=\sqrt{mgh/k}$.
Reports the equilibrium compression $mg/k$ instead of the maximum compression.
Uses the result for a block placed on the spring and released from its top, $x=2mg/k$.
At maximum compression $mg(h+x)=\tfrac12kx^2$; with $m=1.5$ kg, $h=0.4$ m and $k=200$ N/m the positive root is $x=0.327$ m.

ap_physics_1-m04.stem: A $0.5\text{ kg}$ pendulum bob hangs from a light string of length $2\text{ m}$. The bob is pulled aside until the string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical and is then released from rest. What is the speed of the bob at the lowest point of its swing? Ignore air resistance.

options.why: Drops the factor of two from the energy equation, $\sqrt{gL(1-\cos\theta)}$.
Uses $L\sin\theta$ as the height lost, $\sqrt{2gL\sin\theta}$.
Uses the full string length as the height lost, $\sqrt{2gL}$.
The bob drops $L(1-\cos30^\circ)=0.268$ m, so $v=\sqrt{2gh}=2.29$ m/s, independent of the mass.

ap_physics_1-m05.stem: The graph shows the potential energy $U$ of a particle as a function of position $x$. The only force on the particle is the conservative force associated with this potential energy. What is the $x$-component of the force on the particle while it is between $x=0\text{ m}$ and $x=2\text{ m}$?

stimulus.description: Potential energy of a particle versus position

options.why: Takes the force equal to the slope of the graph instead of the negative of the slope.
Reports the change in potential energy over the interval without dividing by the distance.
Reads the force on the neighboring segment instead of the stated interval.
The slope on this interval is $(12-0)/(2-0)=6.00$ J/m, so $F_x=-dU/dx=-6.00$ N, directed toward $-x$ where the potential energy is lower.

ap_physics_1-m07.stem: A crane lifts a $400\text{ kg}$ load straight upward. At one instant the load is moving upward at $1.5\text{ m/s}$ and is accelerating upward at $0.5\text{ m/s}^2$. What is the instantaneous power delivered to the load by the cable at that instant?

options.why: Forgets the mass and uses $(g+a)v$.
Subtracts the acceleration from $g$, $m(g-a)v$, as if the load were accelerating downward.
The tension is $T=m(g+a)=4120$ N, so $P=Tv=6180$ W.
Uses only the net force, $mav$, and forgets that the cable must also support the weight.

ap_physics_1-m09.stem: A $0.5\text{ kg}$ ball is dropped from rest from a height of $1.5\text{ m}$ onto a hard floor. After the first bounce it rises to a maximum height of $1.2\text{ m}$. How much mechanical energy is dissipated in the bounce? Ignore air resistance.

The top of the incline is $1.5\text{ m}$ above the bottom, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $0.2$. options.why: Ignores friction, $\sqrt{2gh}$.

The slope length is $L=h/\sin\theta=3.55$ m, so $\tfrac12mv^2=mgh-\mu mg\cos\theta\,L$ gives $v=4.10$ m/s.

stimulus.description: Energy bar charts of the block-Earth-ramp system

options.text: Energy was destroyed during the slide, because the kinetic energy is less than the initial potential energy.

options.why: Applies conservation of mechanical energy to a slide in which the chart shows an internal energy bar.

ap_physics_1-m21.stem: Two blocks of mass $2\text{ kg}$ and $4\text{ kg}$ are released from rest at the same height of $1\text{ m}$ on the same frictionless incline, one after the other. Which statement about the two blocks at the bottom of the incline is correct?

options.text: The $4\text{ kg}$ block is faster, because a larger mass pulls harder on the incline.
options.why: Believes a larger mass falls faster, ignoring that the mass cancels in the energy equation.

options.text: The speeds are equal and the kinetic energies are equal, because both blocks lose the same height.
options.why: Equates the same height with the same energy, forgetting that the energy lost is $mgh$ and scales with the mass.

options.text: The $2\text{ kg}$ block is faster, because it is easier to accelerate.
options.why: Mixes up the acceleration with the net force; on a frictionless incline both accelerate at the same rate.

options.text: The speeds are equal, and the $4\text{ kg}$ block has $2$ times the kinetic energy of the $2\text{ kg}$ block.
options.why: The speed $\sqrt{2gh}$ does not depend on the mass, while the kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$ is proportional to the mass.

ap_physics_1-m24.stem: A worker pulls a $60\text{ kg}$ crate across a level floor at a constant speed of $2\text{ m/s}$ with a horizontal rope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.2$. What is the power the worker delivers to the crate?

options.why: Uses the friction coefficient times the speed times $g$ and forgets the mass.
Multiplies the friction coefficient by the mass and speed, omitting $g$.
Computes the kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2$ instead of the power.
At constant speed the pull equals the friction force $\mu mg=118\text{ N}$, so $P=Fv=235\text{ W}$.

ap_physics_1-m25.stem: A block slides at $6\text{ m/s}$ onto a rough horizontal patch of length $2\text{ m}$ with a kinetic friction coefficient of $0.2$. What is its speed when it leaves the patch?

options.why: Uses the friction work as if it were the final kinetic energy per unit mass.
Ignores friction and reports the initial speed.
$\tfrac12mv_0^2-\mu mgd=\tfrac12mv^2$ gives $v=\sqrt{6^2-2(0.2)(9.8)(2)}=5.31\text{ m/s}$.
Subtracts the friction work from the speed instead of from the kinetic energy.
